events.credibility_reason: Only the abstract was readable; the content of the claimed 'prime classification' extension is unknown, so what the thesis actually establishes beyond composite-producing k-classes cannot be confirmed.

why: Read literally, the statement asks whether every admissible triple yields infinitely many primes, and it already fails before the snapshot: classical Sierpiński/Riesel numbers (e.g. k·2^n+1 with a covering set, divisor gcd(k+1,1)=1) are admissible triples with no prime values at all. Composite-for-all-n results on fixed k (Filaseta–Groth–Luckner, Groth's thesis, Evans et al. where the k are fixed numbers of the form tb^t+α, Bispels et al., Virbalas) therefore exhibit further counterexample triples for a claim already known to fail; per F4 these move the frontier rather than settle anything, so I scored them bound with null direction while recording the objects as counterexamples. Single record primes are instances. Cullen-form results (multiplier tied to exponent), two-variable a^m−b^n, and the conditional almost-all-composite result are variants. Grantham–Granville is a heuristic: none. No AI involvement anywhere. Groth's thesis counts as digested via committee approval (F9), but its unread prime-classification claim makes it doubtful.
doubts: The close call is the composite-family events: they could alternatively be read as 'case' (settling specific triples negatively, direction refuted), which would give a misleading 'partial, refuted' status dated 2025–26 for a statement literally refuted decades earlier; or as 'none' if the list item implicitly excludes covering-set triples. The researcher read Evans et al. as outside the form, but the Sierpiński/Riesel numbers there are fixed k values, so I treated it as in-family. The literal statement's falsity rests on classical Sierpiński numbers not recorded as events, so open_stale is not available from the record.
